title: ECTODERMAL DYSPLASIA 17 WITH OR WITHOUT LIMB MALFORMATIONS

relationships.phenotype: ECTODERMAL DYSPLASIA 17 WITH OR WITHOUT LIMB MALFORMATIONS

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that ectodermal dysplasia-17 with or without limb malformations (ECTD17) is caused by heterozygous or homozygous mutation in the LEF1 gene (153245) on chromosome 4q25.

checks.claim: Ectodermal dysplasia-17 with or without limb malformations (ECTD17) is caused by heterozygous or homozygous mutation in the LEF1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We provide further evidence for LEF1 haploinsufficiency role in ectodermal dysplasia and delineate its clinical phenotype.
checks.explanation: The abstract supports heterozygous (haploinsufficient) LEF1 deletions causing ectodermal dysplasia. It does not mention homozygous mutations, limb malformations, or the ECTD17 designation.

checks.claim: The LEF1 gene is located on chromosome 4q25.
checks.evidence_quote: We report two unrelated patients with 4q25 de novo deletion encompassing LEF1
checks.explanation: The deletion at 4q25 contains LEF1, which places the gene at 4q25.

paragraphs.text: Ectodermal dysplasia-17 with or without limb malformations (ECTD17) is a disorder of ectodermal development. Its features include severe oligodontia, hypotrichosis, and hypohidrosis (Levy et al., 2020). Some patients also have limb malformations such as radial ray defects, polydactyly, or split hand/foot (Dufour et al., 2022). Severity ranges from mild to moderate with monoallelic LEF1 variants to severe with biallelic variants (Dufour et al., 2022).

checks.claim: Ectodermal dysplasia-17 with or without limb malformations (ECTD17) is a disorder of ectodermal development.
checks.evidence_quote: LEF1 haploinsufficiency causes ectodermal dysplasia.
checks.explanation: The paper describes the LEF1-related disorder as an ectodermal dysplasia, a disorder of ectodermal development. The ECTD17 name is just nomenclature.

checks.explanation: The abstract names all three features.

checks.claim: Some patients with ECTD17 have limb malformations such as radial ray defects, polydactyly, or split hand/foot.
checks.evidence_quote: The phenotypic spectrum includes various limb malformations, such as radial ray defects, polydactyly or split hand/foot, and ectodermal dysplasia.

checks.claim: ECTD17 severity ranges from mild to moderate with monoallelic LEF1 variants to severe with biallelic LEF1 variants.
checks.evidence_quote: haploinsufficiency or loss of DNA binding are responsible for a mild to moderate phenotype, whereas loss of β-catenin binding caused by biallelic variants is associated with a severe phenotype.
checks.explanation: Haploinsufficiency/loss of DNA binding (monoallelic) gives mild-moderate; biallelic gives severe.

paragraphs.text: Dufour et al. (2022) described 11 affected individuals from 4 unrelated families with monoallelic LEF1 variants and 1 affected individual from a consanguineous family with a biallelic LEF1 variant. The phenotypic spectrum included ectodermal dysplasia and various limb malformations, such as radial ray defects, polydactyly, or split hand/foot. The authors found that the biallelic variant was associated with a severe phenotype.

paragraphs.text: The 4q25 deletions that encompassed LEF1 in the 2 patients reported by Levy et al. (2020) occurred de novo, which fits autosomal dominant inheritance. Dufour et al. (2022) found monoallelic LEF1 variants in 11 affected individuals from 4 families and a biallelic variant in an affected individual from a consanguineous family. They stated that inheritance can be either autosomal dominant or autosomal recessive, depending on the type and location of the LEF1 variant.

paragraphs.text: In 2 unrelated patients with hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia, Levy et al. (2020) identified de novo heterozygous deletions at 4q25 that encompassed the LEF1 gene. The authors said their findings gave further evidence that LEF1 haploinsufficiency plays a role in ectodermal dysplasia. They noted that no pathogenic variants involving LEF1 had previously been reported in humans.

paragraphs.text: Dufour et al. (2022) detected monoallelic (heterozygous) variants in the LEF1 gene in 11 affected individuals from 4 unrelated families with ectodermal dysplasia and/or limb malformations. In an affected individual from a consanguineous family, they detected a biallelic (homozygous) LEF1 variant. The authors used immunofluorescence, immunoblotting, pulldown assays, and RNA sequencing to study the variants. Transcriptomic studies showed altered WNT signaling associated with the LEF1 variants.
